meaning: The number 775 appears in the Bible in connection with the silver accounting of the tabernacle and with returning families after the Babylonian exile.
description: 775 appears in the Bible in at least two places. In Exodus 38:25, 1,775 shekels of silver are mentioned as collected from those registered in the congregation, calculated according to the sanctuary weight. The silver was used to cast the bases of the tabernacle and for the hooks on the pillars, linking the number to the construction of God's sanctuary. In Ezra 2:5, the number of descendants of Arah who returned from the Babylonian exile is given as 775, as part of the detailed census of those returning home. Although 775 has not received a distinct symbolic role in traditional Jewish numerology or gematria, these occurrences give the number a place in biblical narratives about sanctuary service and restoration after exile.

versions.meaning: The number 775 has no well-established or known symbolic meaning in biblical or Jewish tradition.
versions.description: 775 is not a number highlighted in the Bible or in traditional Jewish numerology (gematria) with any specific symbolic meaning. Although one can find Hebrew words or phrases that sum to 775 in gematria, it is not a number that has gained any prominent or widely recognized symbolic role in these traditions. It also does not appear as a notable number in biblical narratives or prophecies.

These provide context and make the description more informative and precise.; [minor] The Meaning field is very dismissive. footnotes.text: In Exodus 38:25–28, the exact use of the silver is described: 100 talents for the bases of the tabernacle, and the remaining 1,775 shekels for hooks, overlays, and crossbars for the pillars. The level of detail underscores the precise accounting related to the materials of the sanctuary.

Arah (ארח) means 'traveler' or 'wayfarer'. In Ezra 2:5, his descendants are listed as 775, while the parallel passage in Nehemiah 7:10 lists 652 – a difference that has been the subject of textual critical discussion.
The censuses in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 were compiled to document the legitimacy and inheritance rights of the returning families in rebuilt Israel after the Babylonian exile (around 538 B.C.).
